sections.heading: What's Wrong, and What We Do About It
body: Here is what Wichita homeowners call about, the likely cause, and what we do.

items.title: The house won't get below 80
items.text: A Wichita summer works an air conditioner hard, and the usual causes are a failed capacitor or fan motor, a clogged coil or a refrigerant leak. Nate finds the part that failed and replaces it, or finds the leak instead of just adding more refrigerant.

items.title: The outdoor unit hums and never starts
items.text: A weak capacitor or contactor gives the motor no start-up jolt, and the motor itself may be fine. We swap the small part and test the system through a full cycle.

items.title: The furnace clicks but never lights
items.text: Usually a worn igniter or a sensor coated in soot or dust, and both are small parts. We replace the one that failed, and we tell you if what we find is bigger than a part.

items.title: Cooling fades a little more every week
items.text: That points to a slow refrigerant leak, which can take more than one visit to chase down. We stop the leak, explain which part has to be ordered, and keep the system running in the meantime where we can.

items.title: One room never gets comfortable
items.text: Either the main system was never sized for that room, or the ducts leak or run through an unheated space. We install mini splits for rooms the system doesn't reach, and we do ductwork.

items.title: The furnace is old and the repairs keep stacking up
items.text: A part replaced two winters running, or a water heater tank rusted at the base, means the unit is wearing out. Nate tells you when a repair still makes sense and when a new furnace or water heater is the better spend.

sections.heading: What You Notice, and What It Means
body: Wichita houses run a heater hard from November to March, and a cold snap is when a worn one finally quits. Before you call, check the filter and the thermostat, and look at the base of the water heater for water.

items.title: Cold rooms and uneven heat
items.text: A blower that's wearing out, a clogged filter or leaking ducts can cause it, and so can a furnace that can't keep up any more. We look at the blower, the filter and the ducts first, and tell you which one it is.

items.title: A furnace that starts and stops
items.text: It's short-cycling: often too big for the house, so it heats fast and shuts off, or it's overheating from a dirty filter or a failing part. We find which, and replace the part or size a new furnace to the house.

items.title: A cold shower halfway through
items.text: Tanks collect sediment, especially in hard water, and it covers the bottom of the tank and the heating element or burner. We tell you whether it's the element, the burner or the tank itself.

items.title: Water around the base of the tank
items.text: The tank is leaking from the inside, and a leaking tank can't be repaired. We install a new water heater and take the old one out.

tail: If you're not sure which unit is the problem, call and tell us what's happening.

sections.heading: Repair or Replace
body: Replace when the heat exchanger has cracked, because that part can't be fixed safely. Replace when a water heater tank is leaking.
Replace when the unit is old and the repairs are stacking up. A rule of thumb: if a repair costs a big share of a new unit, the money is better spent on the new one.
Repair when one part has failed and the rest of the unit is in decent shape. An igniter, a blower motor or a thermostat can all be swapped without replacing the furnace.
Nate will tell you which one yours is. We also repair what's in your house, so a repair is an answer you can hear from us.

sections.heading: What We Install
list: **Furnaces,** as replacements for units that have failed or aged out.
**Water heaters,** including heat pump (hybrid) models, which pull heat from the surrounding air to heat the water and cost less to run than a standard electric tank.
**Heat pumps,** for homes that want heating and cooling from one system.
body: The job starts with what's in the house now: where the old unit sits, how it's vented and what it's connected to.

sections.heading: Why the Install Matters
body: A good heater installed badly is still a bad heater. A furnace that's too big short-cycles and wears out early. One that's too small never catches up on a January night.
Sizing comes from the house: its square footage, its insulation, its windows and its ducts. The old unit's size is only a starting point, because the house may have changed since it went in.
Venting is the part people don't see. A gas furnace or water heater has to send combustion gases outside, and a poor connection can put them in the house.
That's why a gas appliance is worth getting installed by someone you can call back. If something smells or sounds wrong afterward, you want to reach the person who set it up.

sections.heading: What You Hear, and Which Part It Is
body: Moving parts wear out first, and the ones that work hardest wear fastest. In Wichita that's a hot summer on the condenser fan and a long winter on the furnace blower.

items.title: The unit hums but won't start
items.text: A weak capacitor or contactor, which give a motor its start-up jolt. The motor itself may be fine, so we swap the small part first.

items.title: The outdoor fan or the blower stalls
items.text: The motor bearings have worn, and dust and heat speed that up. We replace the motor with one that matches the unit.

items.title: The furnace clicks and quits
items.text: An igniter or a sensor, most often. The igniter cracks after many heat cycles, and a dirty sensor can't prove the flame, so we replace or clean the one that failed.

items.title: Cooling slowly fades
items.text: A leak in a refrigerant line or a coil lets refrigerant out, and ice on the lines or a hissing sound is a clue. We find the leak and repair it, not just top off the system.

tail: The fix is usually to swap the failed part and test the system through a full cycle. A capacitor or contactor is a quick swap. A motor takes longer, because it has to match the unit.
Why replace a motor rather than the unit? A motor is one part in a system built from many. If the compressor, coils and controls are sound, the system has plenty of life left.

sections.quote: 2 years in a row has saved us from cooking after our AC went out in the middle of summer. Both times was quick, he knew exactly the issue with little investigation and got it resolved. Absolute necessity with toddlers inside.

sections.heading: A Leak Takes More Than One Visit
body: Topping off refrigerant without finding the leak just starts the clock again. The system runs low, cools badly and strains the compressor, which is the most expensive part to lose.
A slow leak can take more than one visit to chase down. Coils corrode over time, and fittings and joints can weep a little at a time.
Sometimes the part has to be ordered. We explain what failed and what's needed, and we do what we can to keep the system running in the meantime.

sections.quote: He came over and fixed our air conditioner within an hour of being called. I have little kids so I’m sure glad they were able to work us in their schedule. I’m so appreciative!

sections.heading: Fix the Part or Replace the System
body: A part is the right answer when the rest of the system is in decent shape. It's the wrong answer when the unit is old and failing in several places, or when the compressor or heat exchanger has gone.
Check how many times it's been fixed lately. One part in a long-running system is a repair. A second or third failure in a short span means the system as a whole is wearing out.
Nate will tell you which one you're facing. If replacement makes sense, we install furnaces, water heaters and air conditioners too.

sections.quote: Was very surprised when Nathan said he would be able to make it over to repair furnace motor just a few hours after contacting him. He had it done in no time and will now be my go to on any hvac needs.

sections.heading: Maintenance That Catches It Early
body: Most parts don't fail without warning. Filters clog, bearings get noisy, coils collect dirt, and the system works harder until something gives.

Cottonwood fluff and yard dust can coat the outdoor coil by midsummer, and a dirty coil makes the system run longer and hotter. A clean filter, a clear space around the outdoor unit and an ear for new noises catch most trouble early.
We do maintenance on heating and cooling equipment, so small problems are found before they become a dead system on the hottest or coldest day of the year.
In winter, the same goes for the furnace: a clean filter, clear vents and a look at the flame. A steady blue flame is what you want to see. Yellow or flickering is worth a call.

items.q: Do I need a whole new system?
items.a: Not always. Many failures come down to one part. Call and describe what it's doing, and Nate can tell you whether it sounds like a part or something bigger.

items.q: Do you fix furnaces and air conditioners?
items.a: Yes, both, and heat pumps and water heaters.
Yes. Tenants and landlords both call.
Yes. Text what the unit is doing, and Nate will answer.

items.q: What should I check before I call?
items.a: The thermostat setting, the breaker and the air filter. Then tell Nate what the unit is doing, because that narrows down the part.

items.q: Why does the unit hum but not start?
items.a: Usually a weak capacitor, which gives the motor its start-up jolt. It's a small part, and it's often the whole problem.

items.q: Can the same part fail again?
items.a: A new part in a worn-out system can. That's why the repair-or-replace question comes up when failures start to pile up.
